stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In a three-year study of upland meadows, ecologist Moira Lindqvist compared plots heavily browsed by red deer with plots where browsing was light. Where deer were abundant, they stripped away the low shrubs that ground-nesting birds such as meadow pipits use to conceal their nests, and pipit nesting success fell sharply. Nuthatches and tits nesting in tree cavities at the plot edges, however, fared equally well under both conditions. Lindqvist's results suggest that fencing deer out of a heavily browsed meadow would most likely ______
choices: increase nesting success among ground-nesting birds but have little effect on cavity-nesting birds.
increase nesting success among cavity-nesting birds but have little effect on ground-nesting birds.
decrease nesting success among ground-nesting birds but have little effect on cavity-nesting birds.
increase nesting success among both ground-nesting birds and cavity-nesting birds.
explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: heavy browsing → shrubs lost → ground-nester success falls, while cavity nesters are unaffected. Fencing deer out reverses the condition, so the shrubs and their cover should return. The group that was harmed, ground nesters, should recover, and cavity nesters, who were never affected, should show little change.

B.why: You got the direction right but attached it to the wrong group. The passage says cavity nesters fared the same under both conditions. Ground nesters were the ones that depended on shrub cover.

C.why: You picked the right group but the wrong direction. Browsing lowered pipit success, so removing the browsing should raise it, not lower it further.

D.why: You assumed that what helps one group helps every group. Cavity nesters showed no response to browsing, so nothing in the passage supports a gain for them.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many public health officials have assumed that a tax on sugary drinks reduces consumption about equally across a population. A study of one midsize city's two-cent-per-ounce soda tax complicates that view. After the tax took effect, soda purchases fell substantially in low-income households, for which the price increase was a noticeable share of grocery spending, but barely changed in high-income households. The study's findings suggest that if the city repealed the tax, ______
choices: purchases in high-income households would likely rise, while those in low-income households would change little.
purchases in low-income households would likely rise, while those in high-income households would change little.
purchases in low-income households would likely fall further, while those in high-income households would change little.
purchases in low-income and high-income households would likely rise by roughly similar amounts.
explanation: The finding: tax → purchases fall in low-income households, with little change in high-income ones. Repealing the tax removes the price increase. The group that responded, low-income households, would likely buy more again, and the group that barely responded would likely stay about the same.

A.why: You swapped the groups. High-income purchases barely moved when the tax arrived, so there is little reason to expect them to move when it leaves.

C.why: You kept the right group but missed that repeal reverses the change. Taking away the price increase should push purchases back up, not down.

D.why: You fell back on the popular view the passage sets up only to undercut. The study found the two groups responded very differently, so an equal response to repeal isn't supported.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Ceramic coatings are widely applied to turbine blades on the assumption that they reduce wear at any operating temperature. Materials engineer Tomas Okafor found otherwise. Above about 600°C, his coating fused into a hard, glassy layer, and coated blades wore far more slowly than uncoated ones. Below that temperature, the coating remained powdery, and coated and uncoated blades wore at the same rate. Okafor's results suggest that in an engine redesigned so that its blades run at 450°C instead of 700°C, ______
choices: coated blades would likely wear more slowly than uncoated blades.
coated and uncoated blades would likely wear at about the same rate.
coated blades would likely wear faster than uncoated blades.
coated blades would likely wear even more slowly than at 700°C.
explanation: The finding splits at 600°C. Above it, the coating forms a glassy layer and slows wear. Below it, the coating stays powdery and gives no advantage. At 450°C the redesigned engine is below the threshold, so coated and uncoated blades should wear at about the same rate.

A.why: You applied the high-temperature result to a low-temperature case. A wear advantage appears only above 600°C, and 450°C falls in the half of the finding where it disappears.

C.why: You overshot the change. Below 600°C the passage reports equal wear, not faster wear for coated blades. Losing an advantage is not the same as gaining a disadvantage.

D.why: You added an assumption the passage doesn't contain: that cooler running improves the coating's performance. The passage says that below 600°C the coating does nothing to reduce wear.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many marine larvae drift for weeks before choosing a place to settle. Arashiro's findings suggest that if speakers playing healthy-reef recordings were installed on a degraded, quiet reef, ______

oyster larvae would likely settle there in smaller numbers, while mussel settlement would change little.
oyster larvae and mussel larvae would both likely settle there in noticeably greater numbers.
oyster larvae would likely settle there in greater numbers, while mussel settlement would change little.
explanation: The finding: reef sound → more oyster settlement, with no effect on mussels. Adding reef sound to a quiet reef applies that condition, so oyster settlement should rise and mussel settlement should stay about the same.

A.why: You attached the effect to the wrong species. Mussels settled at the same rate with or without sound. Oysters were the ones that responded.

B.why: You picked the right species but reversed the direction. Oysters were drawn toward reef sounds, so adding those sounds should increase their settlement, not reduce it.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Cartographers often add shaded relief (simulated shadows that make hills appear three-dimensional) on the assumption that it helps every reader judge terrain. Fairweather's results suggest that removing the shaded relief from a hiking map would likely ______

improve novice readers' accuracy in judging elevation while leaving experienced readers' largely unchanged.
reduce novice readers' accuracy in judging elevation while leaving experienced readers' largely unchanged.
reduce novice and experienced readers' accuracy in judging elevation by similar amounts.
explanation: The finding: shaded relief → better elevation judgments for novices, with no difference for experienced readers. Removing it takes away the aid, so novices should become less accurate. Experienced readers, who rely on contour lines, should be largely unaffected.

B.why: You picked the right group but the wrong direction. Novices did better with shading, so taking it away should lower their accuracy, not raise it.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Chloride from road salt seeps into concrete bridge decks and rusts the steel reinforcing bars inside. In a ten-year field study, civil engineer Rosa Delacroix found that heavy salting sharply accelerated rebar corrosion in decks made of ordinary concrete. In decks sealed with a waterproof membrane beneath the pavement, however, corrosion proceeded at the same slow rate seen in unsalted ordinary decks, whether the road above was salted or not. Delacroix's findings imply that where winter roads are heavily salted, a deck built with the membrane would likely ______
choices: corrode faster than an otherwise identical deck built without a membrane.
corrode at about the same rate as an otherwise identical deck without one.
corrode more slowly than an otherwise identical deck built without a membrane.
show no corrosion at all, unlike an otherwise identical deck without one.
explanation: Under heavy salting, the ordinary deck's corrosion is sharply accelerated, while the membrane deck stays at the slow, unsalted rate. Comparing the two under the same salted conditions, the membrane deck should corrode more slowly.

A.why: You swapped which deck is protected. Salt accelerated corrosion only in the ordinary decks, so the membrane deck is the slower one.

B.why: You ignored the condition the question names. The two decks corrode at similar rates only without salt. With heavy salting, the ordinary deck speeds up and the membrane deck doesn't.

D.why: You read 'no effect from salt' as 'no corrosion.' The passage says membrane decks still corroded, just at a slow rate.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: It is often claimed that eighteenth-century musicians simply favored slower tempos than modern performers do. Musicologist Anika Brandt argues instead that the room mattered. Comparing tempo markings that composers revised when works moved between venues, she found that in highly reverberant churches, fast passages were marked noticeably slower, probably so that rapid notes would not blur in the echo. Slow movements, however, kept their original markings. Brandt's findings suggest that if a lively dance movement written for a small salon were moved to a cathedral, it would likely ______
choices: be marked at a slower tempo, while a slow movement moved along with it would keep its marking.
keep its marking, while a slow movement moved along with it would be marked at a slower tempo.
be marked at a faster tempo, while a slow movement moved along with it would keep its marking.
be marked at a slower tempo, and a slow movement moved along with it would be slowed as well.
explanation: The finding: reverberant venue → fast passages marked slower, while slow movements stay unchanged. A lively dance moving into a cathedral meets exactly that condition, so it should be slowed. A slow movement on the same program would keep its marking.

B.why: You swapped which kind of movement changes. Brandt found that fast passages were slowed and slow movements were left alone.

C.why: You picked the right movement but the wrong direction. Echo blurs rapid notes, so composers slowed fast passages rather than speeding them up.

D.why: You extended the slowdown to every movement, which is the popular view Brandt argues against. The passage says slow movements kept their original markings.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Etchers have long dampened paper before printing, believing that moist paper picks up ink better from every part of a plate. Conservator Ilse Marchetti tested that practice. On dampened paper, ink transferred far more completely from deeply bitten lines than it did on dry paper, but shallow, lightly bitten lines printed equally well on both. Marchetti's results suggest that if an etcher who had always used dampened paper switched to dry paper, ______
choices: the shallow lines would likely print less fully, while the deep lines would print about as well as before.
the deep lines would likely print more fully, while the shallow lines would print about as well as before.
both the deep lines and the shallow lines would likely print noticeably less fully than before.
the deep lines would likely print less fully, while the shallow lines would print about as well as before.
explanation: The finding: dampening → fuller ink transfer from deep lines, with no difference for shallow lines. Switching to dry paper removes that benefit, so the deep lines should print less fully and the shallow lines should look about the same as before.

A.why: You swapped the line types. Shallow lines printed equally well on dry and damp paper. Only the deep lines depended on dampening.

B.why: You picked the right line type but the wrong direction. Dampening helped deep lines, so dropping it should make them print less fully, not more.

C.why: You accepted the traditional belief that the passage sets up to test. Marchetti found that shallow lines were unaffected by dampening, so they shouldn't get worse on dry paper.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many cartographers treat the scale bar as a formality. They assume readers judge distance from familiar landmarks rather than from the bar itself. A 2023 study by geographer Lina Okafor complicates that view. Participants estimated walking distances on city maps printed with and without a scale bar. Removing the bar had no measurable effect on the estimates of participants who knew the city well, but participants unfamiliar with the city overestimated distances by about 30 percent. Okafor's results suggest that printing a tourist map without a scale bar would likely ______
choices: lead longtime residents to judge destinations as farther away than they really are.
lead visitors new to the city to judge destinations as closer than they really are.
lead visitors new to the city to judge destinations as farther away than they really are.
lead visitors new to the city to avoid walking to most of the destinations shown.
explanation: Write the finding as one arrow: no scale bar → distances overestimated → only for readers unfamiliar with the city. A tourist map is read mainly by visitors who don't know the city, so taking off the bar should push their estimates up. They would see destinations as farther away than they are. Only this choice gets both the group and the direction right.

A.why: You got the direction right but picked the wrong group. The passage says removing the bar had no measurable effect on people who knew the city well, so longtime residents are the group the study found unaffected.

B.why: You got the group right but flipped the direction. Unfamiliar readers overestimated distances, so they would judge destinations as farther away, not closer.

D.why: You added a step the passage never takes. The study measured distance estimates, not whether people chose to walk, and 'most of the destinations' claims more than the evidence supports.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Economists Teodor Vance and Asha Mbeki tested at forty regional firms whether a compressed schedule changes how often workers quit. Under this schedule, employees work four ten-hour days instead of five eight-hour days. Over eighteen months, quit rates among employees without caregiving duties held steady. Quit rates among employees who cared for children or older relatives, however, fell sharply. If these results hold, a firm that abandoned a compressed schedule it had already adopted would potentially ______
choices: see fewer resignations among its employees who have caregiving duties.
see more resignations among its employees who have caregiving duties.
see more resignations among its employees who lack caregiving duties.
see most of its employees resign, whether or not they have caregiving duties.
explanation: The finding as one arrow: compressed schedule → fewer quits → caregivers only. The question runs that arrow backward because the firm removes the schedule. If adopting the schedule lowered caregivers' quit rate, abandoning it would potentially raise that rate again. Only this choice has the right group and the right direction.

A.why: You picked the right group but kept the original direction. The firm is ending the schedule, so the effect reverses: caregivers' resignations would rise, not fall.

C.why: You got the direction right but chose the wrong group. Quit rates for employees without caregiving duties held steady under the schedule, so the study gives no reason to expect a change for them when it ends.

D.why: This is strength creep. The passage supports a change in how often one group quits, not 'most' employees leaving, and it found no effect at all for people without caregiving duties.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many dietitians assume that eating protein before carbohydrates blunts the post-meal rise in blood sugar for everyone. In a 2024 trial, however, nutrition scientist Priya Raman found that the protein-first order substantially lowered blood-sugar peaks in participants with prediabetes, while participants with normal glucose regulation showed no measurable change. Raman's findings suggest that if a clinic serving mostly patients with normal glucose regulation began recommending protein-first meals, ______
choices: its patients' blood-sugar peaks would likely stay about the same as before.
its patients' blood-sugar peaks would likely fall well below their earlier levels.
its patients' blood-sugar peaks would likely climb well above their earlier levels.
its patients' blood-sugar peaks would likely fall further than those of prediabetic patients.
explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: protein-first order → lower blood-sugar peaks → only in people with prediabetes. For people with normal glucose regulation, the trial found no measurable change. The clinic in the question serves mostly that second group, so the most the passage supports is that their peaks would stay about the same.

B.why: You got the direction right but applied it to the wrong group. The drop in blood-sugar peaks showed up only in participants with prediabetes. This choice uses the dietitians' 'works for everyone' view, which the passage sets up specifically so it can reject it.

C.why: You flipped the direction of the effect. Nothing in the passage says the protein-first order raises blood sugar for anyone. The group in question showed no change, not an increase.

D.why: This choice reverses which group benefits. Participants with prediabetes saw the substantial drop and the normal-regulation group saw none, so the clinic's patients can't drop further than the prediabetic patients.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Astronomers have often assumed that a red dwarf star's flare activity depends chiefly on its mass. A survey of several hundred red dwarfs led by astrophysicist Tomás Ibarra, however, found that flare frequency fell sharply as the stars aged, whereas stellar mass showed no clear relationship to flare frequency. These results suggest that a planet orbiting an older red dwarf would likely ______
choices: experience fewer flares than a comparable planet orbiting a younger red dwarf.
experience more flares than a comparable planet orbiting a younger red dwarf.
experience fewer flares than a comparable planet orbiting a lower-mass red dwarf.
be spared all flares, unlike a comparable planet orbiting a younger red dwarf.
explanation: The arrow is: older star → lower flare frequency. Mass has no effect. Apply that to a planet whose star is older: it should see fewer flares than a planet around a younger star. Only this choice keeps both the variable (age) and the direction (fewer) right.

B.why: You picked the right variable but reversed the direction. Flare frequency falls as red dwarfs age, so the planet around the older star should see fewer flares, not more.

C.why: You switched to the wrong variable. The survey found no clear link between mass and flare frequency, so comparing stars by mass brings back the older assumption the passage undercuts.

D.why: This is strength creep. The passage says flare frequency 'fell sharply', not that it reached zero. Fewer flares supports 'fewer', not 'none'.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Wastewater from oil production is often pumped deep underground, a practice seismologists have linked to swarms of small earthquakes. Analyzing records from dozens of disposal wells, geophysicist Hana Okafor found that earthquake rates rose when fluid was injected into rock layers lying directly on top of crystalline basement rock, but not when it went into layers separated from the basement by thick shale. Okafor's findings suggest that if an operator redirected its wastewater from a layer directly above basement rock into one sealed off by thick shale, ______
choices: the earthquake rate near that well would likely decline.
the earthquake rate near that well would likely increase.
the earthquake rate near that well would likely stay unchanged.
the earthquake rate across the whole region would drop to zero.
explanation: The arrow is: injection directly above basement rock → higher earthquake rate. Injection behind thick shale → no rise. The operator is moving from the condition that raises the rate to the one that doesn't, so the extra earthquakes tied to that well should fall away. The rate near the well would likely decline.

B.why: You reversed the direction of the change. Moving injection away from the layer that triggered more earthquakes takes away the cause. It doesn't make the cause stronger.

C.why: You applied 'no rise' to the wrong starting point. The shale layer produces no increase, but this well starts out injecting into the layer that had raised the rate. Switching layers removes that increase, so the rate shouldn't stay where it was.

D.why: This is strength creep on two counts. The finding is about one well's injection, not every earthquake in the region, and 'likely decline' can't be stretched to 'drop to zero'.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Dietary fiber is often promoted as a way to steady blood sugar for everyone. A 2023 feeding trial, however, found a narrower effect. Adults with insulin resistance, who typically show sharper afternoon blood-sugar spikes than adults with normal insulin sensitivity, had markedly smaller spikes after switching to a high-fiber breakfast, while adults with normal sensitivity showed no change at all. If both groups adopted the high-fiber breakfast, the trial's results suggest that the difference in spike size between the two groups would likely ______
choices: widen, because spikes would shrink among adults with normal insulin sensitivity.
narrow, because spikes would shrink among adults with insulin resistance.
widen, because spikes would grow among adults with insulin resistance.
disappear, because spikes in both groups would fall to the same size.
explanation: Write the finding as one arrow: high-fiber breakfast → smaller spikes → only in adults with insulin resistance. That group starts out with the larger spikes, so when its spikes shrink and the other group's stay the same, the distance between the two groups gets smaller. You need the right direction (narrow) and the right group (insulin resistance), and only this choice has both.

A.why: You got the direction of change right but gave it to the wrong group. The passage says adults with normal sensitivity showed no change, so their spikes can't be the ones that shrink. This is the swapped-group trap.

C.why: You picked the right group but flipped the direction. Fiber made spikes smaller for adults with insulin resistance, not larger, so the gap can't widen for this reason.

D.why: You went from 'markedly smaller' to 'the same size.' The passage says the spikes shrank, not that they shrank enough to match the other group. Equal spikes is an extra assumption.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: A common assumption holds that folktales lose their violence once they are written down. However, folklorist Ilse Brandvold's study of recorded performances found that print made little difference. What mattered was the audience: tellers performing before children routinely cut violent episodes, whereas the same tellers kept them when only adults listened. In one valley, harvest-festival tellings and evening tellings in private homes had long matched closely, since both drew adult audiences. When the festival opened to families in 1960 but home gatherings stayed adult-only, the gap in violent episodes between the two settings likely ______
choices: grew, with the household tellings containing fewer violent episodes.
shrank, with the festival tellings containing more violent episodes.
grew, with the household tellers adding violent episodes to compensate.
grew, with the festival tellings containing fewer violent episodes.
explanation: Write the finding as one arrow: children in the audience → violent episodes cut. In 1960 only the festival gained children, so festival tellings would lose violent episodes while home tellings stayed the same. The two settings started out close together, so the gap grew, and it is the festival that has fewer violent episodes.

A.why: You got the direction right (the gap grew) but put the drop in the wrong setting. Home gatherings stayed adult-only, and adult-only tellers kept their violent episodes. This is the swapped-group trap.

B.why: You picked the right setting but flipped the effect. Children in the audience lead tellers to cut violent episodes, not add them. The settings also started out matched, so there was no gap left to shrink.

C.why: You added a step the passage never takes. Nothing says home tellers reacted to the festival change. The passage only says adult-only tellings kept their violent episodes.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because Mercator maps stretch landmasses more and more toward the poles, they are widely assumed to distort viewers' sense of size everywhere on the map. A 2021 study complicated that view: students using a Mercator map greatly overestimated the areas of high-latitude countries, yet their estimates for equatorial countries were accurate. Asked to compare two countries of equal true area, one near the equator and one near the Arctic, these students judged the northern one far larger. Had the students used an equal-area map instead, the gap between their two estimates would most likely have ______

shrunk, because estimates for the equatorial country would increase.
widened, because estimates for the high-latitude country would increase.
vanished, because students would then judge every area exactly.
explanation: Write the finding as one arrow: Mercator stretching → overestimates → only for high-latitude countries. An equal-area map takes away the stretching, so the inflated estimate for the northern country should come down, and the equatorial estimate, which was already accurate, should stay put. The gap shrinks because the high-latitude estimate falls.

B.why: You got the direction right but credited the wrong country. The equatorial estimates were already accurate, so the map change gives them no reason to move. This is the swapped-group trap.

C.why: You picked the right country but flipped the direction. Mercator inflated the northern country's size, so taking away the distortion would lower that estimate, not raise it.

D.why: You went from 'less distorted' to 'perfectly accurate.' The passage gives no evidence that an equal-area map removes all estimation error. 'Every area exactly' claims far more than the study shows.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Historians long assumed that the flying shuttle, introduced to English looms in 1733, sped up all hand weaving about equally. Guild records analyzed by historian Mira Calloway, however, suggest otherwise. The device roughly doubled daily output for weavers of broadcloth, a wide fabric that had previously required two workers to pass the shuttle back and forth, but it left output for weavers of narrow cloth essentially unchanged. If Calloway is correct, a workshop that adopted the shuttle while making only narrow cloth would NOT have ______
choices: seen its daily output of cloth rise substantially.
gained less from the device than broadcloth workshops did.
produced roughly as much cloth each day as before.
used a device once thought to speed all weaving.
explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: flying shuttle → output doubles → broadcloth only. For narrow cloth, output stayed essentially the same. A narrow-cloth workshop therefore would not have seen its output rise substantially, so A is what it would NOT have done. The other three choices all describe things that did happen to such a workshop.

B.why: This is the swapped-group trap. If you gave the doubling to narrow cloth instead of broadcloth, you'd think a narrow-cloth workshop gained more, so 'would NOT have gained less' sounds right. But the passage puts the gain on broadcloth, so a narrow-cloth workshop did gain less, and this choice can't complete a NOT statement.

C.why: You got the direction wrong. The passage says narrow-cloth output was 'essentially unchanged,' so the workshop did produce about as much as before. Saying it would NOT have done so contradicts the finding.

D.why: This is true. The workshop did adopt the shuttle, which historians once thought sped up all weaving. But it has nothing to do with the finding the blank applies, and since it's true, it can't be the thing the workshop would NOT have done. You probably spotted a true statement and stopped reading.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Economists studying a city's 2019 paid-sick-leave mandate found that it reduced quitting among hourly restaurant workers by about 20 percent. Turnover among salaried restaurant managers, nearly all of whom already received paid leave from their employers before the law, did not change. The economists attribute the hourly workers' drop in quitting to the leave itself. If the city were to repeal the mandate, then, the economists would most likely NOT expect ______
choices: managers to start leaving their jobs far more often.
hourly workers to start quitting more often than before.
managers' turnover to stay close to its earlier level.
hourly turnover to shift more than managers' turnover.
explanation: The arrow is: paid leave → less quitting → hourly workers only. Managers already had leave from their employers, so the law didn't affect them. Repealing it reverses the arrow for hourly workers, whose quitting should rise, and does nothing for managers. The economists would therefore NOT expect managers to start leaving far more often.

B.why: This is the reversed-direction trap. Taking away a benefit that reduced quitting should raise quitting, so the economists would expect this. If you thought repeal would lower quitting further, or would leave it alone, this looked like the thing they wouldn't expect.

C.why: Managers' turnover didn't move when the law arrived, because they already had paid leave. It has no reason to move when the law goes. The economists would expect it to stay put, so it can't complete a NOT statement.

D.why: This is the swapped-group trap. The hourly group is the one the law affected, so repeal should change hourly turnover more than managers' turnover. If you mixed up which group the law affected, you'd think this was unexpected.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many planners assume that restored wetlands guard against flooding in every storm. A hydrologist tracking twelve restored sites in one river basin, however, found that the wetlands cut peak stream flows by nearly a third during moderate storms but barely reduced them during the heaviest storms, when the surrounding soils were already saturated and could absorb no more water. If heavy storms come to make up a larger share of the basin's rainfall, the wetlands' flood protection would most likely NOT ______
choices: reduce peak flows in a larger share of storms.
help in a smaller share of the basin's storms.
continue to cut peak flows in moderate storms.
matter least in storms falling on saturated soil.
explanation: The arrow is: restored wetlands → lower peak flows → moderate storms, not the heaviest ones. If heavy storms make up more of the rainfall, more storms fall into the group the wetlands barely help. Their protection would cover a smaller share of storms, not a larger one, so A is what it would NOT do.

B.why: This is the reversed-direction trap. More heavy storms means more storms the wetlands barely help, so their protection would reach a smaller share of storms. That is the expected result. If you had the shift going the other way, this looked like the thing that wouldn't happen.

C.why: The finding about moderate storms still holds. Wetlands cut their peaks by nearly a third, and nothing in the change affects that. You'd expect this to continue, so it can't fill a NOT blank.

D.why: This is the swapped-group trap. The heaviest storms, the ones falling on saturated soil, are where the wetlands help least. If you mixed up which storms the wetlands help, you'd think this was the thing that wouldn't be true.
